_note: Case files for 'Open a Case File'. Each case points to an object in data/objects.json (objectId). The object's purpose, story and status are reused from that record. Every evidence item quotes or summarises a NASA source, linked by URL. Questions are answered only from that evidence. All sources are listed in docs/research-sources.md. `claims` power the Detective workspace: each claim is classified as confirmed, interpretation (reasonable interpretation), possibility (unconfirmed possibility) or unknown, with an explanation that points to the case's own evidence source. `unknowns` lists what remains uncertain.

cases.codename: The mirror that never switched off
cases.hook: It has no power supply at all. So how can scientists still be using it more than 50 years after it was left on the Moon?

evidence.label: Catalogue record
evidence.text: NASA's catalogue lists the laser reflector as part of Apollo 11's early experiment package, but notes that it "was not attached to the unit and required no power."

evidence.label: Engineering note
evidence.text: The panel holds 100 "corner cubes" in a 46 cm aluminium frame. Each one reflects a beam of light straight back to where it came from.
evidence.sourceName: NASA Goddard: Measuring the Moon's Distance

evidence.label: Status report
evidence.text: NASA's 2011 guidance for future Moon missions says the Apollo 11 reflector "continues to be an active scientific experiment" and could be easily damaged by dust or chemical contamination.
evidence.sourceName: NASA's Recommendations to Space-Faring Entities (2011), p. 18

evidence.label: Measurement log
evidence.text: Observatories time laser pulses bounced off reflectors like this one, measuring the Earth–Moon distance to within a few millimetres.
evidence.sourceName: NASA: The Apollo Experiment That Keeps on Giving

cases.question: Laser measurements using reflectors like this one revealed something about the Moon's orbit. What is the Moon doing?
options: Moving closer to Earth by about 3.8 cm a year
Moving away from Earth by about 3.8 cm a year
Staying at exactly the same distance
Moving away from Earth by about 3.8 metres a year
cases.answer: Moving away from Earth by about 3.8 cm a year
cases.explanation: NASA's Moon fact sheet lists the Moon's "recession rate from Earth" as 3.8 cm per year. Laser ranging can measure the Earth–Moon distance to within a few millimetres, precise enough to track a change that small. The reflector needs no power, so it never stopped working, and NASA's 2011 guidance notes it is still an active experiment that dust and chemical contamination could easily degrade.
cases.significance: A small, power-free instrument left behind by explorers can keep producing science for more than half a century, but only while its site stays undisturbed. Here, protecting a piece of history and protecting an active experiment are the same job.

claims.text: The reflector needs no power to work.
claims.explain: NASA's catalogue says it "was not attached to the unit and required no power."

claims.text: Laser ranging with reflectors like this one can measure the Earth–Moon distance to within a few millimetres.
claims.explain: Stated in NASA's article on the experiment.
claims.sourceName: NASA: The Apollo Experiment That Keeps on Giving

claims.text: Because it needs no power, it can keep working for as long as its surface stays clean and undisturbed.
claims.explain: A reasonable conclusion from two sourced facts (no power needed, and dust or contamination could easily damage it), but it is our reasoning, not a NASA statement.
claims.sourceName: NASA's Recommendations to Space-Faring Entities (2011), p. 18

claims.text: Dust has already reduced how well the Apollo 11 reflector works.
claims.explain: NASA's 2011 guidance warns that dust could easily damage it, but our sources do not report whether, or how much, that has already happened.
claims.sourceName: NASA's Recommendations to Space-Faring Entities (2011), p. 18

claims.text: The total number of laser pulses that have ever hit this reflector.
claims.explain: None of our sources gives this number, so we cannot say. Guessing would be inventing data.
claims.sourceName: NASA: The Apollo Experiment That Keeps on Giving

unknowns: How much the reflector's performance has changed since 1969 is not reported in our sources.
How many measurements have been made with this particular reflector is not given in our sources.

cases.hook: Opportunity drove 45.16 km across Mars over more than 14 years. Then, in June 2018, it stopped talking. What was happening when it sent its last message?

evidence.label: Catalogue record
evidence.text: Opportunity came to rest in a crater about 20 m wide on 25 January 2004. NASA's catalogue records that "the final communication from the rover was received on 10 June 2018."

evidence.label: Power system
evidence.text: Opportunity ran on solar panels. Its twin rover, Spirit, had already gone silent in 2010, after getting stuck in soft sand and failing to get enough sunlight to survive the winter.

evidence.label: Mission summary
evidence.text: NASA Science: "Opportunity last communicated with Earth on June 10, 2018, as a planet-wide dust storm blanketed the solar-powered rover's location on Mars."

evidence.label: Orbital photograph
evidence.text: On 20 September 2018, after the storm had cleared, a camera on Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter photographed the area from about 268 km up. Opportunity appears as a tiny blip.

cases.question: Opportunity was solar-powered. What was happening on Mars when it sent its last message to Earth?
options: It had broken through a crust and got stuck in soft sand
A planet-wide dust storm was blanketing its location
It was being moved by a NASA mission to a new site
It had already lost contact years earlier, in 2010
cases.answer: A planet-wide dust storm was blanketing its location
cases.explanation: NASA records that Opportunity's last message came on 10 June 2018, while a planet-wide dust storm blanketed the solar-powered rover. Getting stuck in sand, and going silent in 2010, is what happened to its twin Spirit. When the dust cleared, an orbiting camera could still spot Opportunity as a blip. Its 45.16 km drive stayed the record for driving on another world until NASA's Perseverance passed it on 11 October 2026.
cases.significance: Opportunity spent years studying the surface of Mars, and in the end the dusty Martian environment it studied ended its mission. Its silent body, still visible from orbit, is now part of the planet's history: a record of how far, and for how long, a human-made explorer could travel on another world.

claims.text: Opportunity's final communication was received on 10 June 2018.
claims.explain: Recorded in NASA's NSSDCA catalogue entry for Opportunity.

claims.text: The dust storm blocked the sunlight its solar panels needed, so it ran out of power.
claims.explain: NASA says the storm blanketed the solar-powered rover when it last communicated. Linking the two as cause and effect is a reasonable reading of that evidence.

claims.text: Opportunity was still visible from orbit after the storm.
claims.explain: A Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter camera photographed it as a tiny blip on 20 September 2018 (NASA image PIA22549).

claims.text: A gust of wind could clean its panels and wake it up one day.
claims.explain: Nothing in our sources says this has happened or will happen. It is a possibility, not evidence.

claims.text: The exact condition of Opportunity's instruments today.
claims.explain: No source in this case describes the state of its instruments after June 2018.

unknowns: The condition of Opportunity's instruments and batteries today is not documented in our sources.
Our sources record its last communication, not the exact moment its systems stopped working.

cases.hook: Only the top half of the lunar module Eagle ever left the Moon. The bottom half is still at Tranquility Base. What was its last job?

evidence.label: Catalogue record
evidence.text: Eagle landed on 20 July 1969 at 20:17:40 UT. NASA's catalogue says the ascent stage "was launched from the Moon at the end of lunar surface operations and returned the astronauts" to the command module.

evidence.label: Contents list
evidence.text: The descent stage held the landing rocket, fuel and oxidizer tanks, water, oxygen and helium tanks, and storage space for the lunar equipment and experiments.

evidence.label: Photograph note
evidence.text: NASA's description of photo AS11-40-5899: the plaque the crew left "was attached to the ladder on the landing gear strut on the descent stage."

evidence.label: Site protection
evidence.text: NASA's 2011 guidance recommends that no future vehicle visit the Apollo 11 site, with an exclusion zone that "extends 75 m from the lunar module descent stage."
evidence.sourceName: NASA's Recommendations to Space-Faring Entities (2011), p. 17

cases.question: When Armstrong and Aldrin left the Moon, what was the descent stage's final job?
options: It flew back to orbit together with the crew
It acted as the launch pad for the ascent stage
It was driven away to explore a new site
It was taken apart and packed for the trip home
cases.answer: It acted as the launch pad for the ascent stage
cases.explanation: Only the ascent stage was launched from the Moon to return the astronauts to the command module. The descent stage, with its landing rocket and the crew's plaque, stayed behind as the launch pad. The challenge's own NASA resources describe descent stages as "left behind as launch pads". In 2009, NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter photographed the landing site from orbit.
cases.significance: The descent stage is more than leftover equipment: it marks the place where people first set foot on another world. NASA's own 2011 guidance calls Apollo 11 "the first instance in human history in which emissaries from this planet visited another body in the solar system" and says the site "requires preservation". Our interpretation: the most important thing future explorers can do here may be to leave it exactly as it is.

explanationSources.name: NASA's Recommendations to Space-Faring Entities (2011), p. 17

claims.text: The descent stage stayed on the Moon and served as the launch pad for the ascent stage.
claims.explain: NASA's catalogue says the ascent stage was launched from the Moon and returned the astronauts; the descent stage stayed behind.

claims.text: The crew's plaque is attached to the descent stage's landing gear.
claims.explain: NASA's description of photo AS11-40-5899 says the plaque was attached to the ladder on the landing gear strut.

claims.text: NASA recommends that future vehicles stay at least 75 m from the descent stage.
claims.explain: NASA's 2011 guidance sets an exclusion zone that extends 75 m from the descent stage. It is a recommendation, not a law.
claims.sourceName: NASA's Recommendations to Space-Faring Entities (2011), p. 17

claims.text: The descent stage is the most important object at Tranquility Base.
claims.explain: A judgement about value. It is reasonable, since it marks the first crewed landing, but it is an opinion, not a documented fact.
claims.sourceName: NASA's Recommendations to Space-Faring Entities (2011), p. 17

claims.text: Its materials are in the same condition today as in July 1969.
claims.explain: No one has examined it up close since 1969, and our sources contain no measurement of its condition.

unknowns: Its physical condition today has not been measured up close since 1969.
Our sources do not say how the Moon's environment has affected its materials.
